details.label: Discussion
details.text: Thunderstorms are evolving along a lee trough in far southwestern ND -- potentially being aided by a passing midlevel wave farther north (evident in WV imagery). An elongated hodograph with clockwise curvature (around 30-40 kt of effective shear) and steep midlevel lapse rates atop lower/middle 60s dewpoints will support organized clusters and supercell structures capable of producing large to very large hail and severe wind gusts. Deep-layer shear oriented perpendicular to the lee trough will initially favor discrete cells, though localized upscale growth into small clusters is possible with time. A watch will be issued shortly

details.label: Discussion
details.text: As of 2130 UTC, widely scattered thunderstorms were ongoing across central MT. New convection was also developing near the WY border. Ascent from an approaching upper trough should continue to support these storms and any new development this evening. Moisture is modest (40s and 50s F dewpoints), but strong diurnal heating has steepened low and mid-level lapse rates enough for moderate destabilization. This will support stronger updrafts as they move eastward over the next couple of hours. 40-50 kt of westerly flow aloft with supercells and some upscale growth into linear clusters. The dry sub-cloud layer and flow aloft will favor severe gusts, especially with clustering. Hail is also possible, especially with any persistent supercells. Given the increasing severe risk, a downstream Severe Thunderstorm Watch is likely needed soon

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Visible satellite imagery shows gradually deepening moist convection along the higher terrain in southeast AZ. To the immediate west over the lower desert, a hot, well-mixed boundary layer has developed with steep low/mid-level lapse rates contributing to MLCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg. Latest short-term guidance indicates a gradual increase in storm coverage and intensity from late afternoon into this evening as activity spreads east into the more favorable thermodynamic environment. A westerly low-level wind component currently being observed by the Tucson VWP may aid in some forward propagational characteristics and resultant cold pool organization with severe wind gusts up to 80 mph being the primary hazard

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Visible satellite and radar imagery indicate thunderstorms increasing in coverage along the CO Front Range and Sangre de Cristo Mountains within a mid-level moisture plume rotating around the northern periphery of an upper high. Objective analysis and the 18Z DDC observed sounding indicate residual capping in place across the adjacent plains of eastern CO with some deepening of cumulus noted along the Raton Mesa. Continued daytime heating will weaken the cap, allowing the mountain storms to spread east into the lower elevations. Additional storm development is also possible along a surface trough over eastern CO into the OK/TX Panhandles. The presence of steep low/mid-level lapse rates and up to 30 kt of deep-layer shear may support episodic storm organization through this evening with the primary hazard being severe wind gusts up to 65-75 mph
